query: The Co-free FeNiCrMn system was selected to reduce cost while retaining the mechanical performance of equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi; prior work reported comparable or better mechanical properties after excluding Co. Research on FeNiCrMn has mainly addressed corrosion, while studies of related high- and medium-entropy alloys examined dynamic responses under tension or compression, different temperatures and strain rates, compositional changes, and the presence of cracks or voids. Those studies established that dynamic properties are sensitive to loading regime and material condition, but their different chemistries and defect states do not identify what governs FeNiCrMn. Under the constraints of retaining the Co-free composition and its strength–ductility balance, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis explains the dynamic behavior of solidified FeNiCrMn across temperature and strain-rate regimes? Define a controlled study capable of testing the hypothesis, its applicable boundaries, the prior findings that support it, and a result that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: In single-phase FCC FeNiCrMn, the temperature- and strain-rate dependence of flow stress and strain-hardening is governed by a competition between dislocation glide/cross-slip and deformation twinning that is controlled by an effective stacking-fault energy (SFE) which decreases with (a) lower temperature and (b) higher applied strain-rate (via limited dynamic recovery).  When the effective SFE falls below ~25 mJ m⁻², rapid partial-dislocation nucleation produces profuse nanotwinning that raises the work-hardening rate; when it is higher, cross-slip and dynamic recovery dominate and hardening is lower.  Thus the dynamic mechanical response across 77–873 K and 10⁻⁴–10³ s⁻¹ is set by the twinning fraction that the SFE allows.
generation.material_initial_state: Equiatomic FeNiCrMn alloy solidified into a single-phase FCC microstructure, recrystallised, average grain size 20–50 µm, no prior deformation, no Co additions.
generation.intervention: Uniaxial compression or tension applied at controlled true strain-rates from 1 × 10⁻⁴ to 1 × 10³ s⁻¹ while holding temperatures at 77 K, 293 K, 573 K, and 873 K.
generation.conditions: Adiabatic heating limited to <30 K by sample geometry for high-rate tests; atmosphere inert to avoid oxidation.
generation.structural_mediator: Volume fraction and thickness of deformation twins (Σ3 boundaries) and associated stacking faults generated during loading.
generation.mechanism: Lower effective SFE (from reduced T or suppressed recovery at high dε/dt) promotes partial-dislocation emission; the high density of low-energy twin boundaries blocks dislocation motion and continuously supplies new twin lamellae, raising instantaneous hardening.  Higher SFE (from elevated T or slow rate) favours full dislocation cross-slip and climb, enabling dynamic recovery that lowers hardening.
generation.predicted_outcome: 1. Yield strength at 0.2 % plastic strain will (a) roughly double when temperature drops from 293 K to 77 K at a fixed 10⁻³ s⁻¹ rate and (b) increase by ≈30 % when strain-rate rises from 10⁻³ to 10³ s⁻¹ at 293 K.  2. The true strain-hardening rate dσ/dε at 5 % strain will correlate linearly with measured twin volume fraction.  3. Twin volume fraction will exceed 15 % at 77 K/10³ s⁻¹ but remain <3 % at 873 K/10⁻³ s⁻¹.
generation.baseline: At 293 K and 10⁻³ s⁻¹ the alloy shows ~300 MPa yield strength, ~900 MPa ultimate tensile strength, and ~45 % uniform elongation with <5 % post-mortem twins.
generation.boundary: Hypothesis applies to equiatomic FeNiCrMn with grain sizes 10–100 µm and no second phases, for temperatures below 0.6 Tm (~900 K) and strain-rates below 10³ s⁻¹ where melting or shock effects are negligible.
generation.uncertainty: Exact SFE values and their quantitative variation with temperature are not yet measured; chemical short-range order may shift the critical SFE threshold, adding scatter.

falsification_experiment.design: Perform interrupted tensile tests at each T–rate combination to 5 % and 15 % true strain, immediately quench to preserve structure, then quantify twin volume fraction by TEM and EBSD.  Correlate twin fraction with flow stress and hardening.
measurements: post-mortem twin volume fraction and twin thickness (TEM)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: The hypothesis is falsified if the measured twin volume fraction does not increase when either temperature decreases or strain-rate increases, or if flow-stress/hardening changes >15 % occur without corresponding changes in twin density (±2 %).
